title: Introduction to Accounting Standards
outcomes: Explain what Accounting Standards are, who issues or prescribes them, and the four aspects they cover.
Describe the ASB's standard-setting process, the number and legal status of AS in India.
Explain the need for global standards, the IASC/IASB history and what IFRS comprises.
Distinguish adoption from convergence and identify carve-outs, carve-ins and terminology changes.
Apply the Ind AS numbering rule and the roadmap for companies, NBFCs, banks and insurers.

meta.exam_tip: Expect theory questions on benefits of AS, the standard-setting process, carve-outs/carve-ins and roadmap applicability; learn the ₹500 crore / ₹250 crore tests and the "no looking back" rule.

concepts.title: What Accounting Standards are and what they cover
body: GAAP — generally accepted accounting principles — is the mix of rules a reporting entity must follow: the authoritative standards set by standard-setting boards plus the accounting methods that are commonly accepted in practice. Internationally the authoritative part is mostly IFRS; in India it is the Accounting Standards (AS) and the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS).

An Accounting Standard is an authoritative written pronouncement on four things for a type of transaction: recognition (whether and when it enters the books), measurement (at what amount), presentation (where and how it appears in the statements) and disclosure (what extra information is given in the notes).

Who issues them: for non-corporate entities (firms, trusts, sole traders, LLPs that follow AS) the AS are issued by ICAI. For companies, it is the Central Government (acting through MCA) that prescribes AS and Ind AS, using its power in section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013.
The aim is narrow the menu of acceptable treatments so that statements of different enterprises can be compared — not to remove every choice, but to keep choices within reason and make them visible.
concepts.analogy: An Accounting Standard is a recipe card for one dish: what goes in (recognition), how much (measurement), how it is plated (presentation) and what the menu card must say about it (disclosure).
concepts.work: When a client asks "can we show this as an asset?", a CA answers from the relevant standard — and checks whether the client is under AS or Ind AS before answering.

concepts.title: Why standards help: benefits and limits
body: Standardises alternative treatments: confusing variations in how the same event is recorded are reduced. Because one policy cannot suit every enterprise, standards still allow some choices — so the policy actually used must be disclosed (AS 1). Example: an enterprise must say whether it used FIFO or weighted average for inventory.
Calls for additional disclosures that the law itself may not require, so readers understand the treatment used.

Improves comparability — intra-enterprise (the same enterprise across years, which needs consistent policies) and inter-enterprise (different enterprises for the same period, which needs similar policies or disclosed differences so users can adjust).

Reduces creative accounting — bending policies to flatter one group of users, e.g. inflating profit by capitalising revenue expenditure or depressing it by writing off capital expenditure. Clear capitalisation rules for borderline items curb this.

Limits to remember: standards are principle-based, so complex transactions still need judgement; and where a standard conflicts with a statute, the statute prevails — and the statements must still give a true and fair picture inside the law.
concepts.analogy: Standards are like a common measuring tape for a whole market: if every shop used its own tape, nobody could compare two pieces of cloth.
concepts.work: Analysts comparing two cement companies first read their policy notes (depreciation method, inventory formula) so the comparison is like-for-like.

concepts.title: How an Accounting Standard is made in India
body: ICAI set up the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) in 1977. ASB includes representatives of industry and industry associations (ASSOCHAM, CII, FICCI), regulators, academics and government departments. Though constituted by the ICAI Council, it is independent in formulating standards. While framing AS it considers IAS/IFRS and adjusts for Indian law, customs, usage and business environment.

The process has eight steps — area identification, study-group draft, circulation to outside bodies, meeting their representatives, exposure draft, consideration of public comments, Council review and issue. See the table.

Under section 133 of the 2013 Act the Government of India may prescribe accounting standards (or addenda) as recommended by ICAI, in consultation with and after examining the recommendations of NFRA (National Financial Reporting Authority).

Earlier, ASB issued Accounting Standards Interpretations (ASIs) to answer application questions; they had the same authority as the standard. Their consensus portions are now merged as "Explanations" to the relevant AS paragraphs — first in the MCA-notified AS and then, to keep both sets in harmony, in ICAI-issued AS too.
concepts.analogy: Making a standard is like drafting a building code: an expert committee drafts, the public and regulators comment, the council approves, and for companies the government gives it the force of law.
concepts.work: CAs comment on exposure drafts through ICAI — a practitioner who spots a practical problem can influence the final standard.

head: Step
What happens
rows: ASB picks the broad area that needs a standard
A study group writes a preliminary draft (objective, scope, definitions, recognition and measurement, presentation and disclosure); ASB reviews it
Draft goes to ICAI Council members and outside bodies — MCA, SEBI, C&AG, CBDT, SCOPE and others — for comments
ASB meets representatives of those bodies to hear their views
Exposure draft (ED) is finalised and issued for public comment
ASB considers the comments and finalises the draft for the ICAI Council
Council considers it and, if needed, modifies it in consultation with ASB
ICAI issues the AS (non-corporate entities); for companies, MCA notifies it under s.133 (Companies Act, 2013) once NFRA has been consulted
blocks.title: Standard-setting steps of the Accounting Standards Board

concepts.title: How many AS, and their legal status
body: ICAI has issued 29 AS so far. Two were withdrawn: AS 6 Depreciation Accounting (on revision of AS 10, now Property, Plant and Equipment) and AS 8 Accounting for Research and Development (on issue of AS 26 Intangible Assets). So 27 AS are in force.

For companies, MCA had notified 28 AS and withdrew AS 6 in 2016, so 27 are notified today under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 (notified 23 June 2021; apply for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2021; they replaced the 2006 Rules). AS 2, 4, 10, 13, 14, 21 and 29 were revised to move closer to Ind AS.

Status: ICAI is not a legislature — it can enforce its standards only on its members, and a standard cannot override a law. Whether compliance is compulsory for an entity depends on the statute governing that entity. Companies that do not follow Ind AS apply the AS notified under the 2021 Rules.

In the study material the AS are grouped by theme rather than number: presentation and disclosure (AS 1, 3, 17, 18, 20, 24, 25), assets (AS 2, 10, 13, 16, 19, 26, 28), liabilities (AS 15, 29), items affecting the statements (AS 4, 5, 11, 22), revenue (AS 7, 9), others (AS 12, 14) and consolidation (AS 21, 23, 27).
concepts.analogy: Think of 29 numbered seats in a hall with two seats (6 and 8) removed: 27 people are still seated, but the seat numbers were never renumbered.
concepts.work: In audit reports a CA states that the statements comply with the Accounting Standards notified under section 133 — the set of 27.

concepts.title: Why the world moved to global standards
body: Raising money abroad: each country has its own reporting rules, so a company raising capital in another market must translate and restate its statements — costly and confusing. Common standards remove much of this.
Comparability for global investors and analysts, who want to compare statements prepared on similar standards; harmonised reporting raises their confidence.

Uniformity and transparency: if the same events produce different numbers under different systems, accounting loses credibility, errors grow and fraud becomes easier. One high-quality global set is in the public interest.

Global investment: convergence supports free flow of capital, lowers the investor's risk of misjudging, makes group reporting easier for multinationals, removes costly restatements and helps companies listed both at home and abroad.
concepts.analogy: A single global standard is like a common plug socket — every appliance works everywhere without an adaptor.
concepts.work: An Indian company planning an overseas bond issue saves time and fees if its statements are already on a globally accepted basis.

concepts.title: IASC, IASB and what "IFRS" includes
body: The International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), a London-based body of professional accountancy bodies, was formed in June 1973 to develop International Accounting Standards (IAS) in the public interest.

After restructuring during 1997–1999, the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) replaced IASC with effect from 1 April 2001. Standards issued by IASC up to 31 March 2001 keep the name IAS; standards issued by IASB from 1 April 2001 are IFRS. IASB did not scrap the old IAS — they continue in force.

So the term "IFRS" covers four things: IFRS issued by IASB; IAS issued by IASC; interpretations of the Standing Interpretations Committee (SIC); and interpretations of the IFRS Interpretations Committee (IFRIC).

IFRS are principles-based — broad rules rather than prescribed treatments. Many jurisdictions require or permit them for listed and public-interest entities, and lenders and regulators increasingly look to them as well.
concepts.analogy: IASC was the old club; IASB is the new management. The new management kept the old rule book (IAS) and keeps adding new chapters (IFRS).
concepts.work: When reading a foreign client's IFRS statements, a CA should remember that "IFRS compliance" includes the older IAS and the SIC/IFRIC interpretations.

concepts.title: Adoption vs convergence; carve-outs and carve-ins
body: A country becomes IFRS-compliant in one of two ways. Adoption: it fixes a timetable from which specified entities must use IFRS exactly as issued by IASB. Convergence: it writes its own high-quality standards aligned with IFRS, accepting some modifications — fully or partly.
India chose convergence, not adoption, after consulting stakeholders: Ind AS follow IAS/IFRS as far as possible, with departures only where considered essential.

Departures are of three kinds. Terminology changes to match Indian law, e.g. "balance sheet" for "statement of financial position" and "statement of profit and loss" for "statement of comprehensive income". Removal of options available under IFRS, for consistency — these do not create carve-outs. Deviations from IFRS principles because India's economic environment differs — these are called carve-outs.
Carve-ins work the other way: they are extra guidance or extra requirements that Indian standards add beyond what IFRS contains.

Benefits of convergence: more investor confidence through transparency and comparability; easier inter-firm and inter-industry comparison; simpler group consolidation; and acceptance of Indian statements by stock exchanges abroad.
concepts.analogy: Adoption is buying a suit off the rack; convergence is buying the same suit and having the tailor alter the sleeves to fit. A carve-out is cloth cut away; a carve-in is a pocket added.
concepts.work: Indian subsidiaries of foreign groups often keep a reconciliation of the main Ind AS-vs-IFRS differences (carve-outs) for group reporting.

concepts.title: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap
body: Ind AS are IFRS-converged standards notified by the Central Government/MCA under the Companies Act framework. They go through ICAI's standard-setting process and are notified after NFRA's statutory recommendation.

Numbering: an Ind AS based on an IAS keeps the IAS number (IAS 16 → Ind AS 16); one based on an IFRS adds 100 (IFRS 1 → Ind AS 101, IFRS 15 → Ind AS 115). IFRS 17 on insurance contracts has its Indian counterpart in Ind AS 117 (the older insurance standard was Ind AS 104).

History: ICAI began moving towards IFRS in 2006. The original plan for 2011 was postponed (tax and other issues). After the July 2014 Budget speech, MCA notified the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 on 16 February 2015: voluntary application from 1 April 2015, mandatory from 1 April 2016 for specified companies.

Special points: companies listed on SME exchanges need not apply Ind AS (they continue with AS unless they choose otherwise); once Ind AS applies there is no going back, even if net worth later falls; companies outside the roadmap keep applying the AS under the 2021 Rules. For NBFCs, Ind AS applies to both consolidated and individual statements and voluntary adoption is not allowed.
concepts.analogy: The roadmap is a lift that only goes up: once a company steps into the Ind AS lift, it cannot step back down to AS.
concepts.work: Each year an auditor re-checks the net-worth tests for unlisted clients and their group companies, because crossing ₹250 crore can bring Ind AS from the next period.

IFRS 5 → Ind AS 105; IFRS 15 → Ind AS 115; IFRS 16 → Ind AS 116

illustrations.q: Using the Ind AS roadmap for companies (other than banks, NBFCs and insurers), state whether each company must apply Ind AS and from when: (a) Kaveri Ltd., unlisted, net worth ₹540 crore as on 31 March 2014; (b) Shivalik Ltd., listed on an SME exchange, net worth ₹70 crore; (c) Narmada Pvt. Ltd., unlisted, net worth ₹310 crore, with no group links to covered companies; (d) Tapti Ltd., a wholly owned subsidiary of Kaveri Ltd., net worth ₹40 crore; (e) Kaveri Ltd. again, whose net worth fell to ₹420 crore in a later year.

jobs.title: Which framework does the client follow?
jobs.role: Audit senior at a mid-size CA firm
jobs.situation: A new unlisted client, Meru Engineering Pvt. Ltd., has net worth of ₹180 crore. Its parent, Meru Holdings Ltd., is listed on the main board of NSE.
steps: Check the parent: listed on a main stock exchange, so it is covered by the roadmap (Phase I or II depending on net worth).
A subsidiary of a covered company follows its parent onto Ind AS, whatever its own net worth.
So Meru Engineering prepares its statements under Ind AS, not AS.
Record the reasoning in the audit file and use the Ind AS checklist.
jobs.takeaway: Never decide AS vs Ind AS from the client's own size alone — look up the group.
jobs.think: Would the answer change if the parent were listed only on an SME exchange?
jobs.answer: Yes. SME-exchange companies are outside the mandatory roadmap, so the parent need not apply Ind AS; the subsidiary (₹180 crore, unlisted) would then continue with AS unless the group opts in voluntarily.

jobs.title: Explaining "true and fair within the law"
jobs.role: Finance manager of a trust-run school
jobs.situation: The trust's governing statute prescribes a specific format that conflicts with an AS requirement.
steps: Follow the statute where it conflicts — a standard cannot override law.
Disclose the departure and its effect so readers still get a fair picture.
jobs.takeaway: Statute first, standards next, and transparent disclosure always.

mcqs.q: For a partnership firm in India, Accounting Standards are issued by:
mcqs.explain: For non-corporate entities such as partnership firms, trusts and sole proprietors, the Accounting Standards are issued by ICAI through its Accounting Standards Board. The tempting trap is MCA: MCA (the Central Government) prescribes standards for companies under section 133, not for firms. NFRA only recommends to the Government. In practice: a CA auditing a firm checks compliance with ICAI-issued AS, subject to the size-based exemptions for smaller entities.
mcqs.topic: What Accounting Standards are and what they cover

mcqs.q: Accounting Standards for companies under the Companies Act, 2013 are prescribed by:
mcqs.explain: Section 133 empowers the Central Government to prescribe accounting standards as recommended by ICAI, after consultation with and examination of recommendations by NFRA. NFRA advises but does not itself prescribe, so "NFRA alone" is the trap. IASB writes IFRS for the world, not Indian law. In practice: an audit report on a company refers to standards "specified under section 133 of the Act".
mcqs.topic: How an Accounting Standard is made in India

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four aspects that Accounting Standards deal with?
mcqs.explain: Standards cover recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of transactions and events. How much tax is payable on a transaction is decided by tax law, not by accounting standards (AS 22 deals only with how the tax expense is accounted). The trap is measurement — it is very much part of a standard. In practice: the same sale may be recognised in the books under AS and taxed on a different basis under the Income-tax Act.
mcqs.topic: What Accounting Standards are and what they cover

mcqs.q: Inter-enterprise comparison of financial statements is meaningful mainly when:
options: Comparable enterprises use similar policies or disclose the differences
The same enterprise uses the same policies every year
Both enterprises have the same auditor
Both enterprises have the same year-end only
mcqs.explain: Inter-enterprise comparison sets different enterprises side by side for the same period, which works only when their policies are similar or the differences are disclosed so users can adjust. The trap is "the same enterprise every year" — that describes intra-enterprise comparison across years, which needs consistency. In practice: an equity analyst adjusts for a competitor's different depreciation method before comparing margins.
mcqs.topic: Why standards help: benefits and limits

mcqs.q: Where an Accounting Standard conflicts with a statute governing the enterprise:
mcqs.explain: A standard cannot override a law. If they conflict, the statute governs, yet the entity keeps aiming at a true and fair picture inside the legal framework, explaining any departure. The tempting trap is "the Accounting Standard prevails" because standards are mandatory — but their mandatory force itself comes from law. In practice: banks follow formats and provisioning norms prescribed by banking law and RBI where these differ from general standards.
mcqs.topic: Why standards help: benefits and limits

mcqs.q: The Accounting Standards Board of ICAI was constituted in:
mcqs.explain: ICAI constituted the ASB in 1977 and it has since led standard-setting in India. 1949 is the year of the Chartered Accountants Act that created ICAI, 2001 is when IASB replaced IASC, and 2013 is the Companies Act. In practice: ASB still issues and revises AS for non-corporates and drives Ind AS formulation for companies.
mcqs.topic: How an Accounting Standard is made in India

mcqs.q: In the ASB's standard-setting process, the exposure draft is issued:
options: For public comments, after views of specified outside bodies are ascertained
After the Central Government notifies the standard
Before the study group prepares any draft
mcqs.explain: The draft is first circulated to Council members and bodies like MCA, SEBI, C&AG, CBDT and SCOPE, their representatives are met, and only then is the exposure draft finalised and issued to invite public comments. The trap is "only to Council members" — an exposure draft is meant for the public. In practice: CA firms submit comment letters on exposure drafts during this window.
mcqs.topic: How an Accounting Standard is made in India

mcqs.q: How many Accounting Standards are currently in force out of the 29 issued by ICAI?
mcqs.explain: Twenty-nine were issued; AS 6 (Depreciation Accounting) was withdrawn on revision of AS 10 and AS 8 (Accounting for Research and Development) on issue of AS 26, leaving 27. The trap is 28 — MCA had notified 28 and then withdrew AS 6 in 2016, so the notified count is also 27. In practice: numbering was never changed, so there is simply no AS 6 or AS 8 in the list.
mcqs.topic: How many AS, and their legal status

mcqs.q: AS 8 on Accounting for Research and Development was withdrawn on the issue of:
mcqs.explain: Research and development expenditure is now covered by AS 26 Intangible Assets, so AS 8 was withdrawn when AS 26 was issued. AS 10's revision led to the withdrawal of AS 6 on depreciation, which is the usual trap. In practice: development costs that meet the AS 26 criteria are capitalised as an intangible asset; research costs are expensed.
mcqs.topic: How many AS, and their legal status

mcqs.q: The Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 apply to accounting periods beginning on or after:
mcqs.explain: The Rules were notified on 23 June 2021 but apply to accounting periods commencing on or after 1 April 2021; they replaced the 2006 Rules. The tempting trap is the notification date, 23 June 2021. 1 April 2015 and 2016 are Ind AS roadmap dates. In practice: a company not on Ind AS refers to "AS notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021" in its policy note.
mcqs.topic: How many AS, and their legal status

mcqs.q: Standards issued by IASC up to 31 March 2001 are known as:
mcqs.explain: IASC's standards issued up to 31 March 2001 are called International Accounting Standards (IAS); IASB, which replaced IASC from 1 April 2001, issues IFRS. IASB kept the old IAS in force rather than withdrawing them. IFRIC is the interpretations committee, not a series of standards. In practice: IAS 16 and IFRS 16 are both live standards — the numbers belong to different series.
mcqs.topic: IASC, IASB and what "IFRS" includes

mcqs.q: The term "IFRS" in the wide sense does NOT include:
options: Accounting Standards issued by ICAI for non-corporates
mcqs.explain: IFRS in the wide sense covers IFRS issued by IASB, IAS issued by IASC, SIC interpretations and IFRIC interpretations. ICAI's AS for non-corporates are Indian standards and form no part of IFRS. The trap is SIC — although the committee no longer exists, its interpretations still count. In practice: a statement of "compliance with IFRS" must respect every one of those four components.
mcqs.topic: IASC, IASB and what "IFRS" includes

mcqs.q: A country writes its own standards aligned with IFRS but keeps some modifications for local conditions. This is:
mcqs.explain: Convergence means developing national standards that align with IFRS, accepting some modifications. Adoption would mean using IFRS exactly as issued by IASB from a fixed date. India followed convergence — Ind AS — after wide consultation. In practice: Ind AS statements are not automatically "IFRS compliant" because of carve-outs, which is why global groups reconcile the two.
mcqs.topic: Adoption vs convergence; carve-outs and carve-ins

mcqs.q: Using "balance sheet" in Ind AS instead of "statement of financial position" is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Wording was changed so that Ind AS terms match the terms used in Indian law; this is a terminology difference and changes no accounting principle. A carve-out is a deviation from an IFRS principle because India's economic environment differs. In practice: Schedule III of the Companies Act still uses "Balance Sheet", so Ind AS adopted the same label.
mcqs.topic: Adoption vs convergence; carve-outs and carve-ins

mcqs.q: Departures in Ind AS that deviate from IFRS principles because of India's economic environment are called:
mcqs.explain: Deviations from IFRS principles made because Indian economic conditions differ from those IFRS assumes are carve-outs. Extra guidance or requirements added over IFRS are carve-ins, which is the usual trap. Removal of IFRS options is a departure but does not produce a carve-out. In practice: auditors of group companies list carve-outs when reconciling Ind AS numbers to IFRS group packs.
mcqs.topic: Adoption vs convergence; carve-outs and carve-ins

mcqs.q: The Ind AS corresponding to IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers is:
mcqs.explain: An Ind AS based on an IFRS takes the IFRS number plus 100, so IFRS 15 becomes Ind AS 115. Ind AS based on an IAS keep the IAS number — which is why Ind AS 15 would be the wrong pick. Ind AS 105 corresponds to IFRS 5. In practice: Ind AS 115 replaced the older revenue guidance; its AS counterparts are AS 7 and AS 9.
mcqs.topic: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap

mcqs.q: An unlisted company has net worth of ₹320 crore. Under the corporate roadmap, Ind AS became mandatory for it from:
mcqs.explain: Phase II (1 April 2017) covers unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more but less than ₹500 crore, which includes ₹320 crore. Phase I (1 April 2016) was for net worth of ₹500 crore or more. 1 April 2015 was only the voluntary start. In practice: auditors keep a net-worth working each year to see whether an unlisted client has crossed the threshold.
mcqs.topic: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap

mcqs.q: A company that applied Ind AS from Phase I sees its net worth fall below ₹250 crore. It must:
options: Follow Ind AS only for consolidated statements
Choose between AS and Ind AS each year
mcqs.explain: Once Ind AS applies, the company must keep following it for all subsequent statements — there is no looking back even if net worth later falls. The trap is "switch back to AS", which the roadmap does not permit. In practice: management should weigh this one-way door before opting in voluntarily.
mcqs.topic: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT required to apply Ind AS as per the study material?
options: An NBFC with net worth of ₹600 crore
An unlisted company with net worth of ₹700 crore
A main-board listed company with net worth of ₹100 crore
mcqs.explain: Urban co-operative banks and Regional Rural Banks are not required to apply Ind AS. An NBFC with net worth of ₹500 crore or more was in NBFC Phase I (2018); an unlisted company with ₹700 crore was in Phase I (2016); every main-board listed company is covered by Phase II at the latest. In practice: RRB audits still use the existing accounting framework and RBI norms.
mcqs.topic: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap

questions.q: What are Accounting Standards? State the advantages of setting Accounting Standards.

model.text: Meaning: Accounting Standards are authoritative written pronouncements on the recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of transactions and events in financial statements. For non-corporate entities they are issued by ICAI; for companies the Central Government (MCA) prescribes AS and Ind AS under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013.

items: They standardise alternative accounting treatments and so reduce confusing variations; the policy actually used is disclosed.
They require additional disclosures that may not be required by law, so users understand the treatment followed.
They make financial statements comparable — over years for the same enterprise and across enterprises — helping investors and lenders decide.
They reduce the scope for manipulation and creative accounting, for example capitalising revenue expenditure to inflate profit.
They add credibility and reliability to financial statements.

scheme.pt: Issuing authority — ICAI for non-corporates; Central Government/MCA under s.133 for companies
Additional disclosures; curbs creative accounting / manipulation

remarks: Answers that list advantages without defining the term lose the first mark.
mistakes: Saying ICAI prescribes standards for companies — for companies they are prescribed by the Central Government under section 133.
tips: Open with a one-line definition naming the four aspects.
Write advantages as separate numbered points.

questions.q: What do you mean by carve-outs and carve-ins in Ind AS? Why did India choose convergence rather than adoption of IFRS?

model.text: India, through the Government in consultation with ICAI, decided to converge with IFRS rather than adopt them as issued by IASB. Convergence means framing national standards aligned with IFRS but with changes where considered essential; adoption would mean using IFRS exactly as issued from a fixed date.

While framing Ind AS, departures from IFRS were made for three reasons: (i) terminology differences to match Indian law, such as "balance sheet" for "statement of financial position"; (ii) removal of certain options to keep statements consistent and comparable — these do not create carve-outs; and (iii) differences in India's economic environment.

Carve-outs are those departures that deviate from the accounting principles of IFRS because the economic conditions in India differ from the conditions IFRS assumes. Carve-ins are extra guidance or extra requirements that Ind AS contain beyond IFRS.

Convergence was preferred because it lets India stay aligned with global standards for comparability and access to global capital while keeping Indian law, business practice and economic conditions in view.

scheme.pt: Terminology differences and removal of options (no carve-out)
Carve-out — deviation from IFRS principles due to economic environment

remarks: Many answers define carve-out correctly but forget that removal of options does not create a carve-out.
mistakes: Treating every departure from IFRS as a carve-out.
tips: Use the three-way classification: terminology, options, economic environment.

questions.q: State, with reasons, whether Ind AS is mandatory for each of the following under the roadmap for companies other than banks, NBFCs and insurers: (a) Ganga Ltd., unlisted, net worth ₹520 crore; (b) Yamuna Ltd., listed on the BSE main board, net worth ₹90 crore; (c) Sutlej Ltd., listed only on an SME exchange, net worth ₹45 crore; (d) Beas Ltd., unlisted, net worth ₹260 crore; (e) Chenab Ltd., unlisted, net worth ₹60 crore, a subsidiary of Ganga Ltd.; (f) Ganga Ltd. after its net worth falls to ₹230 crore in a later year.

summary: AS = authoritative pronouncements on recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure.
Non-corporates: AS issued by ICAI. Companies: AS/Ind AS prescribed by Central Government/MCA under s.133 after NFRA consultation.
Benefits: standardised treatments, extra disclosures, comparability, less creative accounting. Statute prevails over AS.

India: convergence (Ind AS), with terminology changes, removed options, carve-outs and carve-ins.

viva.q: What is an Accounting Standard and which four aspects does it deal with?
viva.model: An Accounting Standard is an authoritative written pronouncement. It deals with the recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of transactions and events in financial statements.

viva.q: Who issues Accounting Standards for non-corporate entities and who prescribes them for companies?
viva.model: For non-corporate entities the Accounting Standards are issued by ICAI. For companies the Central Government, through MCA, prescribes them under section 133 of the 2013 Act, after consulting NFRA.

viva.q: Why are there only 27 Accounting Standards in force when 29 were issued?
viva.model: ICAI issued 29 standards. AS 6 on depreciation was withdrawn when AS 10 was revised, and AS 8 on research and development was withdrawn when AS 26 on intangible assets was issued, so 27 remain.

points.pt: AS 6 withdrawn on revision of AS 10
AS 8 withdrawn on issue of AS 26

viva.q: Distinguish adoption from convergence, and explain carve-outs and carve-ins.
viva.model: Adoption means using IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB from a set date. Convergence means framing our own standards aligned with IFRS with necessary changes; India chose convergence. Carve-outs are departures from IFRS principles because of the Indian economic environment, while carve-ins are additional requirements over IFRS.

points.pt: Convergence — aligned own standards with changes; India chose it
Carve-out — deviation due to economic environment

viva.q: State the numbering rule for Ind AS and the main Phase I and Phase II net worth tests.
viva.model: An Ind AS based on an IAS keeps the same number, and one based on an IFRS adds one hundred, so IFRS 15 becomes Ind AS 115. Phase I from 1 April 2016 covered companies with net worth of 500 crore or more, and Phase II from 1 April 2017 covered other listed companies and unlisted companies with net worth from 250 crore to 500 crore.

cases.title: Advising the Rao group
cases.case: Rao Textiles Ltd. is unlisted with net worth of ₹470 crore. Its subsidiary Rao Dyes Pvt. Ltd. has net worth of ₹35 crore. A family partnership, Rao & Sons, also does business. The group CFO is preparing a note for the board and asks you four questions.

mcqs.q: Rao Textiles Ltd. falls under:
options: Phase II — Ind AS from 1 April 2017
Phase I — Ind AS from 1 April 2016
mcqs.explain: Rao Textiles is unlisted with net worth between ₹250 crore and ₹500 crore, which is exactly the Phase II band, so Ind AS became mandatory from 1 April 2017. Phase I needed ₹500 crore or more. It is a textile manufacturer, so the NBFC roadmap is irrelevant. In practice: the CFO should confirm the net-worth computation used for the test.
mcqs.topic: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap

mcqs.q: Rao Dyes Pvt. Ltd. (net worth ₹35 crore) must:
options: Apply Ind AS along with its parent
Apply AS because its net worth is small
mcqs.explain: A subsidiary of a company covered by the roadmap applies Ind AS from the same date as its parent, whatever its own net worth. The trap is to judge Rao Dyes by its own size. Ind AS, not IFRS as issued, is what Indian companies apply. In practice: group consolidation is far simpler when parent and subsidiary use the same framework.
mcqs.topic: Ind AS: meaning, numbering and the roadmap

mcqs.q: Rao & Sons, the partnership firm, will follow:
options: Accounting Standards issued by ICAI, subject to applicability
mcqs.explain: Ind AS is a framework for companies under the Companies Act. A partnership firm is a non-corporate entity and follows the AS issued by ICAI, subject to the applicability and exemptions for its size. The trap is "no standards" — firms are not outside the standards framework. In practice: a firm's auditor applies ICAI's criteria for classifying non-corporate entities.
mcqs.topic: What Accounting Standards are and what they cover

mcqs.q: If Rao Textiles' net worth later falls to ₹200 crore, it will:
options: Stop preparing financial statements under any standard
Apply Ind AS only to its subsidiary
mcqs.explain: Once Ind AS becomes applicable, a company must follow it in all later statements; a fall in net worth does not allow a return to AS. The trap is "revert to AS", which the roadmap forbids. In practice: the board note should flag that the decision is irreversible.
